about: Source ledger of the Identity and Access Lab: every factual claim on the page, the document and section it comes from, and the date it was checked. tests/identity.test.js checks the RFC numbers and statuses against the RFC Editor.

entries.claim: 401: the request lacks valid authentication credentials; the server MUST send a WWW-Authenticate header with at least one challenge.
403: the server understood the request but refuses to fulfil it; credentials, if provided, are insufficient.
404: no current representation was found, or the server is not willing to disclose that one exists.
OAuth 2.0 lets a third-party application obtain limited access to an HTTP service, on behalf of a resource owner or on its own behalf.
OAuth defines four roles: resource owner, resource server, client, authorization server.
OpenID Connect 1.0 is a simple identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0 that lets clients verify the identity of the end-user.
entries.doc: OpenID Connect Core 1.0 incorporating errata set 2

entries.claim: SAML 2.0 is an OASIS Standard dated 15 March 2005; its most important use case is multi-domain web single sign-on, carried in XML-encoded assertions with identity provider and service provider roles.
entries.doc: OASIS SAML V2.0 (Core, OS, 15 March 2005) and the SAML V2.0 Technical Overview (committee draft 02, 25 March 2008)
entries.section: front matter; overview section on use cases

entries.claim: A JWT is a compact, URL-safe means of representing claims, encoded as a JSON object that is the payload of a JWS or the plaintext of a JWE.
A bearer token can be used by any party in possession of it, in any way another holder could; no proof of key possession is required.
PKCE mitigates the authorization code interception attack on OAuth 2.0 public clients.
TLS 1.3 allows client/server applications to communicate over the Internet in a way designed to prevent eavesdropping, tampering and message forgery; RFC 9846 obsoletes RFC 8446.
The https scheme is for an origin server capable of establishing a TLS connection secured for HTTP communication.
Internet certificates profile the X.509 v3 certificate format.
Authentication is the process of determining the validity of one or more authenticators used to claim a digital identity.
A password is "something you know"; look-up secrets and out-of-band devices are "something you have"; a biometric match serves as "something you are" (and is not an authenticator by itself).
A 403 client SHOULD NOT automatically repeat the request with the same credentials; a request might be forbidden for reasons unrelated to credentials; a server may hide a resource with 404.
Bearer is an authentication scheme: the token is sent in the Authorization header; a 401 carries a WWW-Authenticate challenge.
HMAC is a mechanism for message authentication using a cryptographic hash function in combination with a secret shared key.
Base 64 Encoding with URL and Filename Safe Alphabet replaces + and / with - and _ .
RFC 6151 updates the security considerations for MD5 and HMAC-MD5.
The first collision for full SHA-1 was produced in 2017 (received 28 February 2017).
entries.doc: Stevens, Bursztein, Karpman, Albertini, Markov: The first collision for full SHA-1, IACR ePrint 2017/190

entries.claim: A server sets a cookie with a Set-Cookie header and the browser sends it back on later requests to the same place.

Secure is sent only on https (except localhost); HttpOnly forbids document.cookie access but the cookie is still sent with script-initiated requests; SameSite Strict/Lax/None semantics; Domain omitted means host-only; __Host- requires Secure, no Domain and Path=/.
entries.doc: MDN Web Docs, Set-Cookie; RFC 6265bis draft revision 22 (4.1.3.2 and 5.6.7)

entries.claim: Lax sends same-site cookies with cross-site requests if and only if they are top-level navigations using a safe method.

Argon2id first (m=19456 KiB, t=2, p=1), then scrypt (N=2^17, r=8, p=1), bcrypt legacy (work factor 10+, 72 byte limit), PBKDF2 when FIPS-140 is required (HMAC-SHA256 600,000; HMAC-SHA512 220,000). A unique salt per password.

ASP.NET Core Identity V3 hashing: PBKDF2 with HMAC-SHA512, 128-bit salt, 256-bit subkey, 100000 iterations by default (PasswordHasherOptions.IterationCount); format marker 0x01 then prf, iteration count and salt length as 4-byte values, salt, subkey; stored base64.

Passwords used as a single factor SHALL be at least 15 characters; as part of multi-factor at least 8; verifiers SHOULD permit at least 64; no composition rules; no periodic change; compare against a blocklist; no knowledge-based questions; rate-limit failed attempts.

Session ids need at least 64 bits of entropy (128 bits for ids you make yourself, from a CSPRNG); renew the id after any privilege change; idle timeouts of 2-5 minutes (high value) or 15-30 minutes (low risk); absolute timeouts such as 4-8 hours; the server must invalidate the session at logout.
entries.section: Session ID Properties; Renew the Session ID; Session Expiration

entries.claim: CSRF defences: synchronizer token, signed double-submit cookie, custom request headers, Fetch Metadata (Sec-Fetch-Site) and Origin checks; do not change state on GET; SameSite is defence in depth and does not replace a proper CSRF defence in most deployments.
entries.doc: OWASP Cross-Site Request Forgery Prevention Cheat Sheet

entries.claim: Subdomains of one registrable domain are the same site but different origins; a subdomain takeover can enable CSRF against a cookie-based BFF, and the __Host- prefix stops the cookie being shared with subdomains.
TLS allows client/server applications to communicate over the Internet in a way designed to prevent eavesdropping, tampering and message forgery; RFC 9846 obsoletes RFC 8446 and RFC 5246.

Differences from TLS 1.2: only AEAD ciphers remain; static RSA and DH suites removed so every key exchange provides forward secrecy; handshake after ServerHello encrypted; HKDF key derivation; changes optionally affecting TLS 1.2 (section 1.4).
The full handshake message flow: ClientHello with key_share, ServerHello with key_share, EncryptedExtensions, Certificate, CertificateVerify, Finished, client Finished, application data.
A TLS-compliant application MUST implement TLS_AES_128_GCM_SHA256 and SHOULD implement TLS_AES_256_GCM_SHA384 and TLS_CHACHA20_POLY1305_SHA256; server_name is a mandatory-to-implement extension.
TLS gives no inherent replay protection for 0-RTT data; clients MUST only send early data they deem safe to be replayed.
Traffic analysis and record padding are discussed (appendix F.3 and section 5.4).
TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 are formally deprecated.
X25519MLKEM768 is a hybrid post-quantum key agreement for TLS 1.3 (observed negotiated by curl 8.18 with OpenSSL 3.5.5).
Encrypted Client Hello encrypts a ClientHello under a server public key; the plaintext SNI otherwise reveals the target domain.
HSTS: the Strict-Transport-Security header with max-age and an optional includeSubDomains directive.
The Common Name RDN MUST NOT be used to identify a service; other RDNs of the subject must not be used either.
Certificate fields: version, serial, signature algorithm, issuer, validity, subject, public key, extensions (basic constraints, key usage, extended key usage, subject alternative name).
PEM encapsulation between BEGIN CERTIFICATE and END CERTIFICATE lines of base64-encoded DER.
Reserved certificate policy identifiers: domain-validated 2.23.140.1.2.1, organization-validated 2.23.140.1.2.2, individual-validated 2.23.140.1.2.3.
Messages printed by curl 8.18.0 and OpenSSL 3.5.5 for an untrusted root, a wrong name, an expired certificate and a missing issuer (run against local test servers).

entries.claim: openssl genpkey, req (-x509, -new, -addext, -subj), x509 (-req, -CA, -CAkey, -CAcreateserial, -extfile, -days), verify and s_server flags exist as used.

Kestrel loads a certificate and key from PEM files (X509Certificate2.CreateFromPemFile); the snippet was built with warnings as errors and run in the test suite.
ACME: account, order, challenges (http-01 on port 80, dns-01), finalize with a CSR.
The TLS-ALPN-01 challenge proves control through a TLS handshake.
Maximum validity of subscriber certificates: 398 days before 2026-03-15, 200 days from then, 100 from 2027-03-15, 47 from 2029-03-15; domain validation reuse 200 then 100 days.

Let's Encrypt: tlsserver profile 45 days from 13 May 2026; classic profile 64 days from 10 February 2027 and 45 days from 16 February 2028; authorization reuse falls to 7 hours; opt-in six-day certificates; wildcard issuance must use DNS-01.

entries.claim: OCSP URLs dropped from certificates on 7 May 2025 and OCSP responders turned off on 6 August 2025.
CAA records let a domain holder name the CAs that may issue; ACME Renewal Information tells clients when to renew.
Certificate Transparency version 2.0 (Experimental) describes public append-only logs; platforms such as Android publish policies that require proof of logging.
entries.doc: RFC 9162 and the Android Certificate Transparency policy

entries.claim: Kestrel validates the client certificate chain against the operating system trust store during the handshake, so a client certificate from a private CA needs ClientCertificateValidation (found by running it; not stated on the documentation page).
OAuth 2.0 mutual-TLS client authentication and certificate-bound access tokens.
JWT claims iss, sub, aud, exp, nbf, iat, jti; validation steps; a JWT is a JWS or JWE.
JWS compact serialization; the header parameters alg, typ and kid.
A JWK is a JSON representation of a key; a JWK Set is a list of them.
JWT access tokens MUST be signed, typ at+jwt, claims iss, exp, aud, sub, client_id, iat and jti are required; RS256 must be supported; asymmetric signing is recommended.
Token introspection lets a resource server ask the authorization server about an opaque token.
Ed25519 is the fully-specified algorithm name; EdDSA is deprecated.
An OpenID Connect ID token is a JWT.

Attacks: alg none and RS256 to HS256 confusion (2.1), weak symmetric keys (2.2); mitigations: algorithm allow-list (3.1, 3.2), validate all operations (3.3), kid and jku handling (3.10), issuer (3.8), audience (3.9), explicit typing (3.11), mutually exclusive validation rules (3.12).

OAuth lets a third-party application obtain limited access to an HTTP service; the problems of password sharing it solves (clear-text storage, password authentication, overly broad access, no individual revocation, compromise of any app).
The four roles: resource owner, resource server, client, authorization server; client types confidential and public.
RFC 9700 is the current best practice: PKCE, no password grant, exact redirect URI matching, implicit discouraged.
OAuth 2.1 is an Internet-Draft, revision 16 dated 3 September 2026, replacing RFC 6749 and RFC 6750 in its text.
code_verifier is 43 to 128 unreserved characters; code_challenge is the base64url of the SHA-256 of the verifier; the method S256; the verifier is sent in the token request.

Authorization request parameters response_type, client_id, redirect_uri, scope, state; token request grant_type, code, redirect_uri, client_id; error codes invalid_request, invalid_client, invalid_grant, unauthorized_client, unsupported_grant_type, invalid_scope.

Exact string matching of redirect URIs; clients MUST prevent CSRF; public clients MUST use PKCE and confidential clients SHOULD; S256 is the only method that does not expose the verifier; servers accept a code_verifier only if a challenge was sent; implicit SHOULD NOT be used; password grant MUST NOT be used; refresh tokens for public clients must be sender-constrained or rotated.
The iss authorization response parameter defends against mix-up attacks.
Pushed authorization requests: the client POSTs the request parameters to the authorization server first; from .NET 9 the OpenID Connect handler uses PAR by default when the server supports it.

entries.claim: Client credentials grant: the client authenticates itself and gets an access token with no resource owner; refresh token grant.
Device authorization grant: device_code, user_code, verification_uri, interval; the device polls the token endpoint; errors authorization_pending and slow_down.
Token exchange swaps one token for another with a different audience or subject.
OpenID Connect 1.0 is a simple identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0; the ID token claims iss, sub (at most 255 ASCII characters), aud, exp, iat, auth_time, nonce, acr, amr, azp, at_hash.

SAML 2.0 is an OASIS Standard (15 March 2005) whose main use case is web single sign-on with XML assertions.
Google's discovery document: issuer, authorization, token and key endpoints, RS256, code_challenge_methods plain and S256 (compared live by the test suite).

Validate iss (https://accounts.google.com or accounts.google.com), aud, exp, signature via jwks_uri; use sub, never email, as the identifier; nonce is required; hd is a login-screen optimisation and must not control access; hd claim to be verified.

entries.claim: ABAC is a logical access control methodology where authorization is determined by evaluating attributes of the subject, object, requested operations and, in some cases, environment conditions against policy, rules or relationships.
Zanzibar is a global system for storing and evaluating access control lists, used by Google services such as Calendar, Drive and Photos.

entries.claim: The scope of an access token limits what the client may do; the requested scope may be narrower than what the resource owner could do.

Broken Access Control is number one in the 2025 Top 10; the whole tested set had some form of it; prevention includes deny by default, enforcing record ownership, logging failures and including access control in tests.
OWASP API Security Top 10 2023: API1 Broken Object Level Authorization, API3 Broken Object Property Level Authorization, API5 Broken Function Level Authorization.
